subject: Biology
central_question: How are the chemical constituents of living tissues organised into small molecules, macromolecules, structural polymers, and enzyme-controlled metabolic systems?
in_scope_units: Chemical analysis of living tissue, acid-soluble and acid-insoluble fractions, wet and dry weight, ash, and inorganic constituents.
Small biomolecules including amino acids, sugars, fatty acids, glycerol, lipids, nitrogen bases, nucleosides, and nucleotides.
Primary and secondary metabolites and their biological, ecological, and human uses.
Biomacromolecules and the special behaviour of lipids in the acid-insoluble fraction.
Proteins and their amino-acid composition and biological functions.
Polysaccharides, including cellulose, starch, glycogen, inulin, and chitin.
Nucleic acids and the nucleotide components of DNA and RNA.
Primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary levels of protein structure.
Enzymes, active sites, reaction rates, activation energy, enzyme action, factors affecting activity, enzyme classes, inhibition, and cofactors.
banned_topics: Detailed metabolic pathways of respiration and photosynthesis
Organic reaction mechanisms beyond the chapter's biological classification

known_pitfalls.claim: All elements found in living matter are unique to life.
known_pitfalls.correction: Living and non-living matter contain many of the same elements, but their relative abundances differ.
Individual lipids are small molecules; they appear in the acid-insoluble fraction because membrane fragments form water-insoluble vesicles.

known_pitfalls.claim: A nucleoside contains base, sugar, and phosphate.
known_pitfalls.correction: A nucleoside contains a nitrogenous base and sugar; addition of phosphate forms a nucleotide.
Proteins are heteropolymers because they contain different amino-acid types.
Most enzymes are proteins, but catalytic nucleic acids called ribozymes also exist.

known_pitfalls.claim: Increasing substrate concentration always increases reaction velocity indefinitely.
known_pitfalls.correction: Velocity reaches Vmax when enzyme active sites become saturated.

recommended_example_progression: NCERT Exercise 7: draw and interpret the structure of alanine as an alpha-amino acid.
NCERT Exercises 1 and 5: define macromolecules and explain triglyceride composition.
NCERT Exercises 2 and 4: explain tertiary protein structure and biological uses of proteins.
NCERT Exercises 8–10: connect gums, qualitative biomolecule tests, cellulose, and biological materials.
NCERT Exercise 11: describe enzyme properties, specificity, optimum conditions, activation energy, inhibition, and cofactors.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: Use the end-of-chapter EXERCISES 1–11 for macromolecules, protein structure, triglycerides, amino acids, biomolecule tests, cellulose, and enzyme properties.
